# spax: spatial accessibility and allocation modeling

<!-- badges: start -->
[![DOI](https://zenodo.org/badge/DOI/10.5281/zenodo.23438611.svg)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23438611)
<!-- badges: end -->

`spax` is a modular engine for spatial access and allocation models. Floating
catchment area (FCA) methods and an allocation model share the same inputs
(demand, facility supply and travel times), decay kernels and numeric engine,
so you can:

- compute accessibility surfaces with the FCA family: 2SFCA, E2SFCA, M2SFCA,
  3SFCA and Huff-2SFCA;
- model where people go with a static conditional logit allocation
  (`spec_clm()`) that includes the Huff model (`spec_huff()`) and
  extends it with an outside option for demand that goes elsewhere: evaluate it
  at chosen parameters, fit it to observed use (facility totals or
  origin-to-facility flows), predict for new areas and test supply scenarios;
- compare models, including FCA scores and fitted allocations on the same
  inputs;
- work with several demand groups that compete for the same facilities, such
  as age bands, or people who drive and people who take the bus; a
  group-specific allocation parameter is fitted only from counts recorded by
  group;
- plug in your own decay kernels, fitting losses, weights and spatially
  varying catchments.

The pieces are built to be combined and extended: a new component uses the
same engine rather than a separate code path. Large rasters are read in
blocks, so the FCA functions run in modest memory. The FCA functions are
stable; the allocation functions are experimental and may change in later
versions.

## Install

Use R 4.4.0 or newer. This is the supported dependency and testing floor for
spax 0.6.0. Calls from earlier versions keep working (see the NEWS).

Install version 0.6.0 by its release tag rather than from the repository's
default branch:

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("Songyosr/spax@v0.6.0")
```

The allocation interface is experimental and may change in later versions. For
reproducible work, record the package version and retain the input IDs, units,
observation declaration and saved results. Development continues on the
`develop` branch (`pak::pak("Songyosr/spax@develop")`).

Each release is archived on Zenodo; doi:10.5281/zenodo.23438611 refers to all
versions (version 0.6.0 is doi:10.5281/zenodo.23538560). Cite the version you
used with `citation("spax")`.

Package and function help are available from an installed package. Installations
that include built articles also provide the guides, which follow one reader
journey: Get started, the example data and data preparation, the FCA guides,
then the allocation model (model choice, the workflow and bootstrap
intervals):

```{r installed-guides, eval=FALSE}
# Package overview, and notes on reusing saved results
help(package = "spax")
help("spax-package", package = "spax")
help("allocation-compatibility", package = "spax")

# The guides
browseVignettes("spax")
# When the installation includes built vignettes:
vignette("spax", package = "spax")  # Get started
vignette("cornwall-data", package = "spax")
vignette("model-choice", package = "spax")
vignette("allocation-workflow", package = "spax")
vignette("facility-bootstrap", package = "spax")
```

## Quick start: GP practices in Cornwall

spax ships open example data for the 55 general practices of Cornwall and the
Isles of Scilly: practice locations and GP full-time equivalents (FTE,
excluding GPs in training) in `cornwall_gp`, small areas with registered
residents in `cornwall_lsoa`, small area × practice registrations in
`cornwall_flows` and travel minutes in `cornwall_travel`, plus a WorldPop 2020
population grid and one travel-time layer per practice. The Isles of Scilly
have no road link to the mainland, so this example models mainland Cornwall
only: it drops the islands' practice and small area, and crops the islands
from the grids. `vignette("cornwall-data", package = "spax")` describes each
object, its sources and its licences.

### An FCA accessibility map

An FCA index takes a demand raster, a facility table and one travel layer per
facility, with layer names matching facility IDs. `prep_data()` holds them
together, a specification such as `spec_e2sfca()` declares the index without
data, and `spax()` computes it. This interface is experimental.

```{r fca, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 3.6, fig.alt = "Raster map of the E2SFCA index for mainland Cornwall in GP FTE per 1,000 residents; values are highest in the west of the county and lowest on Bodmin Moor and at the tips of the western peninsulas."}
library(spax)
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Mainland practices, as a plain table
mainland_gp <- cornwall_gp |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()

# Residents per grid cell, and travel minutes with one layer per practice;
# crop both to the mainland (west edge at 6 degrees W)
pop <- read_spax_example("cornwall_pop.tif")
travel_grid <- read_spax_example("cornwall_gp_travel.tif")
mainland <- ext(-6, xmax(pop), ymin(pop), ymax(pop))
pop <- crop(pop, mainland)
travel_grid <- crop(travel_grid[[mainland_gp$practice]], mainland)

# Demand grid, practice table and travel stack, held together
grid_data <- prep_data(
  pop,
  mainland_gp,
  travel_grid,
  id_col = "practice",  # matches supply rows to travel layers
  supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg"
)

# The E2SFCA index with a 10-minute Gaussian decay
fca <- spax(grid_data, spec_e2sfca(decay = decay_gaussian(sigma = 10)))

plot(
  1000 * fca$accessibility,
  axes = FALSE,
  col = hcl.colors(50, "viridis"),
  main = "E2SFCA index, GP FTE per 1,000 residents"
)
```

This is an enhanced two-step FCA index: supply per distance-weighted
population, in GP FTE per 1,000 residents. The 10-minute Gaussian scale is a
choice for this example, not an estimate. The index is a supply-per-demand
score, not a probability that anyone uses a practice. `spax_e2sfca()` remains
the one-call shortcut and gives the same result from the same inputs. See
`?spec_e2sfca` for the other FCA indices, decays and normalization options,
and `summary(fca)` or `plot(fca)` to inspect the result.

### A static CLM fitted to registrations

The allocation model takes numeric vectors and an origin-by-facility travel
matrix, and fits where people choose to go. Here demand is the residents of
each small area registered with any GP practice in England, supply is GP FTE,
and the target is the observed small area × practice registrations. The model
includes an outside option, which here stands for registration with a practice
outside mainland Cornwall (for example in Devon or on the Isles of Scilly); it
is not unmet need.

```{r clm-inputs}
mainland_lsoa <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()

# Travel minutes (small areas x practices), demand and supply, named by ID
travel <- cornwall_travel[mainland_lsoa$lsoa, mainland_gp$practice]
demand <- setNames(mainland_lsoa$registered, mainland_lsoa$lsoa)
supply <- setNames(mainland_gp$gp_fte_extg, mainland_gp$practice)

# Align the inputs once; unit labels are recorded, not converted
d <- prep_data(
  demand = demand,
  supply = supply,
  travel = travel,
  metadata = list(
    demand_units = "registered residents",
    demand_period = "July 2026",
    supply_units = "GP FTE excluding GPs in training",
    supply_period = "June 2026",
    travel_units = "minutes"
  )
)
d

# Observed registrations: one row per small area and practice
flows <- obs_flows(
  cornwall_flows,
  origin = "lsoa",
  facility = "practice",
  count = "patients"
)
```

```{r clm-fit, message = TRUE}
# Gaussian travel decay and a fitted outside weight v0 (the defaults),
# fitted to the flows
clm <- spax(d, spec_clm(), observed = flows)
clm
```

`spax()` lines the registrations up with the data. The message says what it
dropped: the counts of the Isles of Scilly small area, which is not in the
data, and the few mainland residents registered at the Scilly practice, who
count towards the outside option. No starts were given, so `spax()` found
them from the data: it scans a grid of travel scales and outside weights and
fits from the best points, as the last line of the print says. The loss is
Poisson, the default of `obs_flows()`. Registrations are a stock rather than
independent events, so treat the loss as a fitting criterion. `summary(clm)`
lists every start; give `starts`, `lower` and `upper` to choose them yourself.

```{r clm-check}
coef(clm)

# The observed counts as aligned with the data (small areas x practices)
observed <- clm$observed$target

# Per cent registered outside mainland Cornwall: observed and modelled
outside <- c(
  observed = 1 - sum(observed) / sum(demand),
  modelled = 1 - sum(fitted(clm)) / sum(demand)
)
round(100 * outside, 2)

# Practice totals: modelled against observed
cor(colSums(fitted(clm)), colSums(observed))
```

```{r clm-check-values, include = FALSE}
sigma_hat <- round(coef(clm)[["sigma"]], 1)
r_totals <- round(cor(colSums(fitted(clm)), colSums(observed)), 2)
```

The fitted Gaussian scale is about `r sigma_hat` minutes: registration is
very local. The printed shares are percentages of registered residents.
Practice totals of the fitted flows correlate at `r r_totals` with the
observed ones. One constant outside weight understates registration outside
mainland Cornwall, which is concentrated in a few areas near the Devon border.

`predict()` returns choice probabilities for requested areas. For the practice
with the largest list, St Austell Health Group, the modelled probability can
be set beside the observed share of each area's registered residents:

```{r clm-map, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 3.6, fig.alt = "Two maps of small areas around St Austell: the observed share of residents registered with St Austell Health Group and the modelled probability; the modelled catchment is centred on the same place but spreads more widely."}
# Choice probabilities for every small area
prediction <- predict(
  clm,
  travel = travel,
  demand = demand,
  outputs = "allocation"
)

# Observed share and modelled probability for one practice, in one table
st_austell <- "Y04957"  # St Austell Health Group
shares <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(
    lsoa = rownames(travel),
    source = "Observed share",
    value = observed[, st_austell] / demand
  ),
  data.frame(
    lsoa = rownames(travel),
    source = "Modelled probability",
    value = prediction$outputs$allocation[, st_austell]
  )
) |>
  mutate(source = factor(source, unique(source)))

# Join to the small-area polygons, and locate the practice
mapped <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  select(lsoa) |>
  inner_join(shares, by = "lsoa")
site <- filter(cornwall_gp, practice == st_austell)
xy <- st_coordinates(site)

ggplot(mapped) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = value, colour = value), linewidth = 0.1) +
  geom_sf(data = site, shape = 21, fill = "white", size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~source) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    name = "Share of\nregistered\nresidents",
    limits = c(0, 1),
    aesthetics = c("fill", "colour")
  ) +
  # A 50 x 40 km window around the practice
  coord_sf(xlim = xy[1] + c(-25000, 25000), ylim = xy[2] + c(-20000, 20000)) +
  labs(title = "Registration with St Austell Health Group (white point)") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(margin = margin(b = 8)))
```

The model reproduces the catchment's location but spreads it more widely than
the observed registrations. Registrations record where residents are
registered, not how often they visit. The population grid (WorldPop 2020) and the registrations (NHS England,
2026) are different sources and dates. Data sources and licences are listed in
`system.file("COPYRIGHTS", package = "spax")`.

### Known outside counts

The fit above sees only the counts at the mainland practices, so the outside
option is fitted without any count of its own. Here the outside count of every
small area is known. Demand is the residents registered with any GP practice
in England, and every registered resident is registered somewhere, so the
residents of a small area who are not registered at a mainland practice are
exactly its outside count: its demand less its counts at the mainland
practices, including the few mainland residents registered at the Scilly
practice. `outside = "known"` declares this, and `spax()` fits the outside
count as one more cell of each small area.

```{r clm-known}
clm_known <- spax(
  d,
  spec_clm(),
  observed = obs_flows(
    cornwall_flows,
    origin = "lsoa",
    facility = "practice",
    count = "patients",
    outside = "known"
  )
)
coef(clm_known)

# Per cent registered outside mainland Cornwall: observed and modelled
areas_known <- as.data.frame(clm_known, type = "origins")
known_shares <- c(
  observed = sum(areas_known$outside_observed),
  modelled = sum(areas_known$outside_modelled)
) / sum(areas_known$demand)
round(100 * known_shares, 2)
```

```{r clm-known-values, include = FALSE}
v0_known <- format(round(coef(clm_known)[["v0"]], 3), nsmall = 3)
v0_before <- format(round(coef(clm)[["v0"]], 3), nsmall = 3)
```

The travel scale hardly moves, but the outside weight rises from
`r v0_before` to `r v0_known`, and the modelled outside share now equals the
observed one: with every outside count known by subtraction (demand minus
the counts), the fit is the multinomial likelihood of each small area's
choices, and a constant outside weight reproduces the total outside count.
Use `outside = "known"` only when demand counts the same people as the
observations, as here: registrations by residence from the same extract and
date. It is not a population estimate; list sizes and population differ by
several percent, and the gap would go straight into the outside counts. The Huff
comparison below uses the flows without outside counts, because the Huff model
has no outside option.

### The Huff model on the same data

The Huff model is the conditional logit without the outside option.
`spec_huff()` specifies it; by default it uses power decay and a fitted
attractiveness exponent `beta`, the usual form of the Huff model. Here it takes
the same Gaussian decay and `beta = 1` as the conditional logit above, so the two
fits differ only in the outside option. Without one, the model sends every
registered resident to a mainland practice, and the counts at the Scilly
practice are dropped.

```{r huff, message = TRUE}
huff <- spax(d, spec_huff(decay = decay_gaussian(), beta = 1), observed = flows)
coef(huff)

# Same flows, loss and inputs; loss differences are measured from the Huff fit
comparison <- compare_allocations(list(huff = huff, clm = clm))
as.data.frame(comparison)[
  c("specification", "parameters", "loss_difference", "count_correlation")
]
```

```{r huff-values, include = FALSE}
compared <- as.data.frame(comparison)
outside_gain <- format(round(-compared$loss_difference[2], 1), nsmall = 1)
```

The outside option moves the travel scale very little (from
`r format(round(coef(huff)[["sigma"]], 3), nsmall = 3)` to
`r format(round(coef(clm)[["sigma"]], 3), nsmall = 3)`
minutes) and lowers the Poisson loss by `r outside_gain`. It lets the model
send `r round(100 * outside[["modelled"]], 2)`% of registered residents outside
mainland Cornwall, against `r round(100 * outside[["observed"]], 2)`% observed.
The Huff model is nested in the conditional logit, so this comparison measures
what the outside option adds on these registrations; it does not by itself
show how residents choose practices.

## Continue the allocation workflow

| Function | Purpose |
|:--|:--|
| `prep_data()` | Align demand, supply and travel by ID once, and record units. |
| `spec_clm()`, `spec_huff()` | Specify a model without data; each parameter is a number (held) or `"fit"` (estimated). |
| `decay_gaussian()`, `decay_exponential()`, `decay_power()`, `decay_custom()` | Declare the decay kernel of a specification, with its `sigma`. |
| `obs_flows()`, `obs_totals()` | Declare observed flows or facility totals, and the loss that fits them. |
| `spax()`, `spax_clm()`, `spax_huff()` | Fit the model, or evaluate it at given values; `coef()`, `fitted()`, `summary()`, `as.data.frame()` and `predict()` read the result. |

For full control, the step functions run the same model one step at a time,
and they accept a result of `spax()`:

| Function | Purpose |
|:--|:--|
| `prepare_allocation()` | Align IDs, record units and support, and prepare compact numeric inputs (`prep_data()` returns the same object). |
| `clm_allocation()` | Declare corrected static CLM with Gaussian, exponential or power travel decay, or a kernel declared with `decay_kernel()`. |
| `huff_allocation()` | Declare the Huff model: the same allocation model without an outside option, with power decay and a fitted attractiveness exponent by default. |
| `fit_allocation()` | Fit a selected output from given starts, or from starts found in the data, and retain diagnostics. |
| `evaluate_allocation()` | Evaluate supplied parameters, including a newly prepared supply scenario. |
| `predict_allocation()` | Predict requested origins against saved facility loads; maps are explicit. |
| `check_fit()`, `compare_fits()` (also `check_allocation()`, `compare_allocations()`) | Compare a fit with simpler models, or fits with each other, on the same loss. |
| `bootstrap_fit()` (also `bootstrap_allocation()`) | Run the separately supported conditional facility-case bootstrap. |

`vignette("model-choice", package = "spax")` compares an FCA index and the
static CLM on the same Cornwall inputs and explains what each output means.

A supply scenario requires preparing the changed system and evaluating it at
the selected parameters. Supply can change attraction, allocation and loads.
This is a model-based comparison, not a causal intervention estimate.

The bootstrap has a narrower scope than fitting: static CLM with a fitted
outside mass `v0` and a decay kernel that is smooth in `sigma` (built in, or
declared with `decay_kernel()`; a fitted `beta` is allowed), complete whole
facility counts and an unweighted Poisson original fit. It requires an explicit
event, reference period and independent-facility sampling declaration. The
Cornwall fit above targets small area × practice flows, so it is outside this
method. `vignette("facility-bootstrap", package = "spax")` supplies a generated
example with all 399 attempts and a paired supply comparison;
`vignette("allocation-workflow", package = "spax")` covers fitting, prediction,
a supply scenario and fresh-session export on the Cornwall data.

Conditional percentile intervals require an eligible original, a complete run
of 399 attempts and at least 380 finite successful values for the quantity.
Failed attempts and successful inner-boundary fits remain visible. Coverage was
evaluated for Gaussian decay with fitted `sigma` and `v0`, in generated
80-origin/40-facility designs under tested fixed-input laws; other kernels and a
fitted `beta` use the same procedure without a separate coverage study. This is
not a universal coverage guarantee or evidence for an application's observation
law. No spatial simultaneous intervals are provided.

## IDs, support and saved results

Keep facility IDs on supply, travel and observations; named axes align
independently. Unnamed inputs are positional. Distinguish known zero demand,
unknown demand and excluded origins. Only included positive demand contributes
to fitted facility loads. For CLM prediction, unknown travel and known absence
(`Inf`) have different meanings; inspect validity flags rather than replacing
all missing values with zero. Declare compatible units and reference periods;
the interface does not convert them.

Use `coef()`, `fitted()`, `summary()`, `plot()` and `as.data.frame()` to inspect
saved allocation results. CSV drops R attributes, so keep an RDS bundle with
declarations and support metadata.
See `help("allocation-compatibility", package = "spax")` before reusing older
private fits: corrected
CLM and legacy `huff_decay` have different output meanings, and older objects
may need regeneration for current prediction/reporting.

Report reproducible issues or discuss larger changes on the

Package code uses the MIT license; see [LICENSE](LICENSE.md). The bundled
Cornwall GP example data are openly licensed third-party material (Open
